title: How to Define Expected Quantum Polynomial-Time Zero Knowledge Simulation
authors: Zhengnan Lai, Nicholas Spooner, and Max Tromanhauser
abstract:
Zero knowledge is formalized via a simulator — i.e., an efficient computation which simulates the view of a (malicious) verifier. The foundational results in constant-round zero knowledge [GMW86,FS90,GK96] all use expected polynomial-time (EPT) simulators, and there is evidence that strict poly-time simulators do not exist for these protocols [BL02]. In the post-quantum setting, we must upgrade the simulator to at least quantum polynomial time (QPT) in order to properly simulate quantum verifiers. Chia et al. [CCLY22] proved a surprising negative result which precludes non-trivial ZK for constant-round protocols with both (strict) QPT and a natural notion of expected quantum polynomial-time (EQPT) black-box simulation. In light of this, Lombardi, Spooner, and Ma [LMS22] introduced a novel EQPT notion, coherent-runtime EQPT or EQPT$_c$, and showed that the [GMW86,FS90,GK96] protocols all allow for EQPT$_c$ simulation.

In this work, we identify a fundamental issue with the definition of EQPT$_c$ simulation, and propose a resolution. In particular, we demonstrate that EQPT$_c$ computation is not necessarily efficient and can, in fact, decide any classical decision problem. This is possible through a freedom of choice in selecting a unitary dilation for an efficient quantum channel. We propose an revised definition which carefully restricts this choice, and prove that the definition preserves the zero knowledge of the [GMW86,FS90,GK96] protocols. Additionally, by upgrading the [GK96] framework to the fully quantum setting, we demonstrate for the first time a constant-round (malicious verifier) zero knowledge proof system for QMA (with EQPT$_c$ simulation).

1        Introduction
This paper is about zero knowledge proof systems (ZKPs) which allow a prover to convince an eﬃ-
cient veriﬁer that a statement is valid without revealing any additional information. Zero knowledge
is formalized via a simulator: an eﬃcient computation which simulates the view of an eﬃcient (ma-
licious) veriﬁer.
An important aspect of that formalization is the notion of computational eﬃciency of the simula-
tor. In the classical setting, the most common cryptographic and complexity-theoretic deﬁnition of
eﬃcient computation is strict probabilistic polynomial time (strict PPT), but many seminal con-
structions of (constant-round) ZKPs are not known to have a strict PPT simulator [GK96, GMW86].
Moreover, there is evidence that strict PPT simulators do not exist for these protocols: constant-

To remedy this issue, the standard classical deﬁnition of zero knowledge permits the simulator to
run in expected polynomial time (EPT), a variable-time randomized computation which halts after
a polynomial number of steps in expectation (but may take any ﬁnite number of steps with positive
probability).
In recent years, advances in quantum computing have led to a reevaluation of classical notions of
eﬃciency and security. For zero knowledge, showing security against quantum adversaries entails
exhibiting a simulator that can simulate the view of any eﬃcient quantum veriﬁer [Wat06]. Natu-
rally, this requires that the simulator be at least a QPT machine. Similarly to the classical setting,
however, there is evidence that strict QPT simulation is insuﬃcient for natural constant-round
ZKPs [CCLY22].1 This raises the question of whether there is a natural computational model for
(black-box) zero knowledge simulation in the quantum setting. Given the classical situation, a
quantum version of EPT would seem a natural candidate. Below, we survey existing attempts at
deﬁning quantum EPT and where they fall short.


1.1    Expected Quantum Polynomial-Time (EQPT) Computation
There is surprising subtlety in formalizing quantum computation with variable running time. How
does a quantum Turing machine (QTM) know when to halt? In Deutsch’s original formulation
[Deu85], QTMs evolve unitarily except that at each step a measurement is made to determine if
the computation has halted. One can deﬁne EQPT in this model as those computations where the
expected time before obtaining a halt outcome is polynomial. Lombardi, Ma, and Spooner [LMS22]
refer to this deﬁnition as “measured-runtime” EQPT or EQPTm (Fig. 1).
Issues with this deﬁnition were initially observed decades ago in the context of the quantum halting
problem. As pointed out by Myers [Mye97], if diﬀerent branches of computation halt at diﬀerent
times, then this measurement will necessarily collapse the state of the machine, preventing useful
interference between those branches. This nuance turns out to be a critical issue for zero knowledge
simulation. Speciﬁcally, Chia et al. [CCLY22] showed that this phenomenon leads to a striking
impossibility: constant-round ZKPs with black-box EQPTm simulation exist only for languages in
BQP.
This raised the question of whether this obstacle can be circumvented by choosing a diﬀerent
“halting scheme”. After some debate [Oza98a, LP98, Oza98b], it became clear that this eﬀect
is inherent. In particular, [LP98] noted that regardless of whether we actually perform the halt
measurement or not, each branch of computation will necessarily become entangled with some
description of its runtime, preventing interference between branches with diﬀerent runtimes.2 Thus,
in the context of zero knowledge simulation, we will need to look beyond standard notions of EQPT.

1.2   Our Contributions
In this work, we point out a ﬂaw in the deﬁnition of EQPTc simulation and propose a resolution. In
this section, we give a brief overview of that ﬂaw and that resolution. With those established, we
then give results on the post-quantum zero knowledge of [GMW86, FS90, GK96] under our revised
deﬁnition.

The problem with the prior deﬁnition. In [LMS22], the authors describe a “canonical”
dilation for an EQPTm computation, which they prove can be eﬃciently approximated; moreover,
they show that any EQPTc circuit as in Fig. 2 which utilizes this dilation can also be eﬃciently
approximated. They then claim that, because unitary dilations are equivalent up to a local isometry
on the ancilla, this property will hold for EQPTc circuits regardless of the chosen dilation. Recall
that the EQPTc circuit cannot access the ancilla except through the dilation, so it may seem natural
that the isometry on the ancilla will not aﬀect the circuit output.

The above already demonstrates an inconsistency in the deﬁnition. This particular example may
seem benign, but in Section 3.1 we describe a more involved example where a particular choice of

Our proposed deﬁnition. In order to resolve this issue, we redeﬁne EQPTc simulation in such
a way that preserves the main results and spirit of [LMS22] while avoiding the above problems.
In the new deﬁnition, an EQPTc zero knowledge simulator is correct only if, for all “reasonable”
dilations of the underlying EQPTm procedure, its output is indistinguishable from the real view
of the veriﬁer. This requires some theory for what constitutes a “reasonable” dilation, and we
introduce a new framework for describing dilations which we call approximate dilation schemes.
An approximate dilation scheme is an oracle circuit such that, when the oracle is instantiated
with an EQPTm computation M , the resulting unitary is a dilation of M . In this way, a dila-
tion scheme describes a black-box strategy for dilating variable-runtime procedures. We focus on
dilation schemes which satisfy the following desirable properties. First, we require that the dila-
tion can be approximated by a series of circuits whose size scales polynomially in the inverse of
the approximation error. In particular, we want that any EQPTc computation using the resulting
unitary dilation can be ε-approximated by replacing the unitary with a circuit of size poly(ε−1 ).
Second, we require that the scheme and its approximations are black-box in M . This prevents
perverse behaviour where the dilation “knows” the computation and can perform it independently
of the transition unitary. In the context of zero knowledge simulation, it ensures that the dilation
respects the black-box access model; and if M is using an oracle, the black-box restriction allows
the approximation to use it as well. This is vital for use in reductions, as will be seen in Section 4.
We describe a dilation as being eﬃciently approximable if it is the result of applying an approximate
dilation scheme to an EQPTm computation. Eﬃciently approximable dilations attempt to capture
the key attributes of [LMS22]’s canonical dilation while avoiding pitfalls where simulatability could
strongly depend on the choice of dilation. We can now redeﬁne EQPTc simulation as follows.
Deﬁnition 1.2 (Informal). A protocol is statistical (resp. computational) zero knowledge with
EQPTc simulation if the simulator is correct for all (resp. eﬃciently approximable) dilations.
Note that in the statistical zero knowledge case the [LMS22] deﬁnition is essentially recovered. This
could be expected because proving statistical indistinguishability does not require reductions to be
eﬃcient. Our ﬁrst result re-establishes the connection between EQPTc ZK and ε-ZK.
Theorem 1.3. Under our revised deﬁnition, ZK with EQPTc simulation implies ε-ZK.
This result is obtained by observing that [LMS22]’s “canonical” dilation for EQPTm computations
satisﬁes the properties of an approximate dilation scheme. With the deﬁnition established, the
remainder of the work is dedicated to reproving the EQPTc -ZK results of [LMS22] under the new
deﬁnition.

Discussion. The ﬂaw we identify in the original deﬁnition of EQPTc , and the complexity of our
revised deﬁnition, point to substantial diﬃculties in deﬁning expected quantum polynomial time for
the purposes of (computational) zero knowledge simulation. Many reasonable candidate deﬁnitions
we tried led to subtle issues when used in security proofs. Thus we view our main question as
open: whether there is a truly natural deﬁnition of eﬃcient simulation in the quantum setting that
recovers negligible simulation error for constant-round protocols. Indeed, this work perhaps serves
as further evidence that the “right” notion of ZK in the quantum setting is ε-ZK: it is much easier
to specify and prove, and suﬃces for all applications of which the authors are aware.

Recall the deﬁnition of a Σ-protocol, which consists of three rounds: commitment, challenge, and

Remark 2.4. Our deﬁnitions in this work refer only to ZK proof systems; i.e., protocols with

(argument systems); the zero knowledge property is unaﬀected.
Deﬁnition 2.5 ([BG20]). A quantum Σ-protocol consists of a three-round protocol between a
prover and a veriﬁer, which takes the following form:
    • In the ﬁrst round, the prover sends an initial quantum register A as a commitment.
    • In the second round, the veriﬁer sends a uniformly random challenge r.
    • In the third round, the prover answers the challenge by sending a register Z.
Importantly, [BG20] gave a zero-knowledge quantum Σ-protocol for the class QMA and its simu-
lator, with non-negligible soundness error.
